02. The Agent Loop and Tool Use: Function Calling, Tool Design, Selection at Scale, and Code-as-Action

Overview

Almost every production agent described publicly between 2023 and 2026 runs the same core mechanism. A language model is called with a prompt and a set of tool definitions. It either answers or emits one or more structured tool calls. A harness runs those calls and appends the results to the transcript. The loop repeats until a stopping condition fires. Anthropic's widely cited definition reduces agents to "LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop" [1]. The OpenAI Agents SDK runner, the Claude Agent SDK, and Hugging Face's smolagents all implement versions of this loop [6][25][16].

The loop itself is simple. The engineering effort has gone into five areas around it, and this chapter covers each:

  1. The function-calling protocol. This covers how tool definitions, calls, and results are encoded in provider APIs, how tool choice is forced or constrained, and how schema adherence is guaranteed (Anthropic Messages API, OpenAI function calling, MCP).
  2. Tool design as an interface discipline. Anthropic calls this the "agent-computer interface" (ACI) [1]. SWE-agent showed it empirically [33][34], and Anthropic's 2025 guide turned it into an evaluation-driven process [2].
  3. Tool selection at scale. When an agent can reach hundreds or thousands of tools, loading every definition harms both cost and accuracy. Responses range from retrieval research (Gorilla, ToolLLM, ToolRet, RAG-MCP) to production deferred loading (Anthropic Tool Search, OpenAI tool search) [3][11][24][28][29][30][31].
  4. Code as the action space. CodeAct, smolagents, Anthropic's Programmatic Tool Calling, "code execution with MCP," and Cloudflare's Code Mode replace one-call-per-turn JSON with generated programs that call tools [14][16][12][4][21].
  5. Error recovery and stopping conditions. These include is_error results, instructive error messages, linters and guardrails, iteration and turn caps, stop-reason handling, compaction, and reliability metrics such as pass^k [9][10][25][36].

Throughout the chapter, a number is attributed to the organization that published it. Vendor figures are internal evaluations unless stated otherwise.

1. Lineage: From Prompted ReAct to Native Function Calling

1.1 ReAct (2022)

Problem. Chain-of-thought reasoning helps models plan, but it is ungrounded. Acting without reasoning cannot adapt plans to what the environment reports.

Design. ReAct interleaves free-text Thought steps with Action steps (calls into an environment or API) and Observation steps (the returned results). It does this in a single prompted trace [26]. Thoughts decompose goals, track subgoal completion, and decide what to retrieve next.

Results. On ALFWorld and WebShop, ReAct beat imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning baselines by 34 and 10 absolute points of success rate, using only one or two in-context examples [26].

Legacy. The Thought/Action/Observation cycle is the direct ancestor of the modern loop. smolagents still describes its CodeAgent as a ReAct-style agent [16].

1.2 Toolformer and Gorilla (2023): learning when and how to call

Toolformer (Meta AI, NeurIPS 2023) trained a model in a self-supervised way to decide which API to call, when to call it, and with what arguments. It needed only a handful of demonstrations per tool. The tools included a calculator, a QA system, search, translation, and a calendar [27].

Gorilla fine-tuned LLaMA for writing API calls over HuggingFace, TorchHub, and TensorHub (the APIBench dataset). It reported surpassing GPT-4 at writing API calls. Pairing the model with a document retriever let it adapt to API documentation that changed at test time and substantially reduced hallucination [28]. This was an early sign that tool knowledge should be retrieved, not memorized. Section 4 returns to that idea.

1.3 Native function calling (2023 onward)

Providers then moved tool use into the API itself. A developer declares tools as JSON Schema objects. The model emits typed tool-call blocks instead of free-text Action: lines. The harness returns typed results that are matched to the calls by ID [8][9][23]. The protocol details matter because they decide which failure modes are even possible.

2. The Canonical Agent Loop

2.1 Reference architecture

                 +-----------------------------------------------+
   user task --> |  context = system + tool defs + history       |
                 +-----------------------+-----------------------+
                                         |
                                         v
                              +--------------------+
                              |   LLM inference    |
                              +----------+---------+
                                         |
               +-------------------------+-------------------------+
               | stop_reason / output classification               |
               +----+-----------------+----------------+-----------+
                    |                 |                |
            end_turn / final     tool_use(s)      max_tokens, pause_turn,
            (no tool calls)           |           refusal, context-exceeded
                    |                 v                |
                    |       +-------------------+      v
                    |       | harness: validate,|   special handling
                    |       | authorize, execute|   (continue, retry,
                    |       | (parallel ok)     |    fallback, compact)
                    |       +---------+---------+
                    |                 |
                    |      tool_result blocks (is_error?) appended
                    |                 |
                    v                 +--> loop (turn counter += 1; check caps)
                 answer

Three implementations show how the vendors fill in the boxes.

  • Anthropic Messages API. A response with stop_reason: "tool_use" contains one or more tool_use blocks, each with an id, a name, and an input [9]. The harness sends the next user message containing a tool_result for every tool_use block, matched by tool_use_id. The result blocks must come first in that message. No message may sit between the call and its result, and adding text after results can produce empty or failed turns [9][10]. Unlike APIs that use a dedicated tool or function role, Claude carries tools inside the ordinary user and assistant messages [9].
  • OpenAI Agents SDK. The runner calls the LLM and classifies its output. A final output ends the loop. A handoff switches the active agent and loops again. Tool calls are executed, their results are appended, and the loop runs again. An output counts as final when it contains text of the desired type and no tool calls. Going past max_turns raises MaxTurnsExceeded [25].
  • smolagents. Memory starts with the user task. On each step, the LLM produces an action, the action is executed, and the result is appended to memory. The loop ends when the task is solved (via a final_answer call) [20][16].

Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK post describes the same loop at a higher level: gather context → take action → verify work → repeat [6]. Its distinctive point is that verification is a first-class part of the loop and not an afterthought (see Section 6.4).

2.2 The hidden cost of tool definitions

Tool definitions are not free metadata. Claude's API builds a dedicated system prompt from the tool definitions, tool configuration, and the user's system prompt [8]. Definitions sit at the front of the context, which affects both token cost and caching:

  • Anthropic reports a five-server MCP setup (GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, Splunk) with 58 tools that uses about 55K tokens before any work starts. It has seen definitions reach 134K tokens before optimization [3].
  • The Manus team calls KV-cache hit rate "the most important metric" for a production agent. Their tasks average about 50 tool calls, with an input-to-output token ratio of roughly 100:1 [22]. They cite cached Claude Sonnet input at $0.30 per million tokens against $3.00 uncached [22]. Because tool definitions sit near the front of the context, editing them mid-task invalidates the cache for everything after them [22].
  • Changing tool_choice on Claude invalidates cached message blocks, although tool definitions and the system prompt stay cached [8].

2.3 Controlling the choice: tool_choice, strict mode, and masking

Anthropic. tool_choice takes four values [8]:

  • auto: the default when tools are present.
  • any: the model must call some tool.
  • tool: the model must call one named tool.
  • none: the default when no tools are present.

Forcing a tool works by prefilling the assistant turn, so no natural-language preamble or thinking block comes before the call [8]. Recent documentation (2026) states that some newer models reject any and tool with a 400 error. For those models it recommends auto combined with strict tool use (strict: true, grammar-constrained decoding that guarantees schema-valid inputs) or structured outputs [8]. The tool search documentation notes that the strict-mode grammar is built from the full toolset, so deferred loading does not force a grammar recompile [11].

OpenAI. OpenAI's function calling uses tools; the older functions parameter is deprecated. tool_choice supports auto, required, and none, plus forcing a specific function. Each result is paired to its call by call_id in the Responses API or tool_call_id in Chat Completions [23]. With strict: true, the schema is pre-processed and generation is constrained to it. Secondary guides report that strict schemas require every property to be listed in required and additionalProperties: false [23]. One practitioner caution applies: strict mode guarantees shape, not business validity. A schema-valid call can still name a city that does not exist, so semantic validation stays in the runtime [23].

Manus: mask, don't remove. Manus gives a production argument against changing the toolset dynamically. Removing a tool mid-task invalidates the KV cache. It also confuses the model when earlier steps still refer to the removed tool, which leads to hallucinated or malformed actions [22]. Manus keeps definitions fixed. A context-aware state machine then masks token logits during decoding to prevent or enforce the selection of certain actions [22]. Commentary on the post notes that most providers and inference frameworks support some form of response prefill, which constrains the action space without touching the tool definitions [22].

  Manus-style action constraint (conceptual)
  +-------------------+     state      +------------------------------+
  | agent state       | ------------>  | allowed action set           |
  | machine           |                | (subset of fixed toolset)    |
  +-------------------+                +--------------+---------------+
                                                      |
  fixed tool definitions (cache-stable prefix)        v
  -------------------------------------------> decoder with logit mask
                                               over disallowed actions

3. Tool Design: The Agent-Computer Interface

3.1 Anthropic, "Building Effective Agents" (Dec 2024)

Thesis. Teams should spend as much effort on the agent-computer interface as on human-computer interfaces [1]. Anthropic offers three heuristics:

  • Put yourself in the model's shoes. If a tool is not obvious from its description and parameters, it is not obvious to the model either.
  • Choose argument formats that are close to text commonly seen on the internet. Avoid formats that need overhead such as counting lines or escaping strings.
  • Poka-yoke the tools, so that mistakes are structurally hard to make [1].

Case study. During Anthropic's SWE-bench work, the model made errors with relative file paths after it had moved out of the root directory. The tool was changed to require absolute paths, and the model then used it "flawlessly" [1].

3.2 SWE-agent: the ACI as an empirical variable (NeurIPS 2024)

Problem. Dropping an LM into a bare Linux shell gives it an interface designed for humans.

Architecture. SWE-agent places custom commands between the model and the repository [34]:

  • a file viewer that shows 100 lines per turn, with scrolling and in-file search;
  • an edit command with an integrated linter that rejects edits leaving the file syntactically invalid;
  • a directory-wide search that lists only the file names containing matches, because extra match context confused the model;
  • an explicit message when a command produces no output: "Your command ran successfully and did not produce any output."

Results. The paper reported 12.5% pass@1 on SWE-bench and 87.7% on HumanEvalFix, which were state-of-the-art for that setup at the time [33]. A secondary summary of the ablations reports roughly 10.7 percentage points more solved issues on 300 SWE-bench Lite instances than an otherwise identical agent with a plain shell [33]. Treat that figure as approximate.

Lesson. The interface is a first-order variable. Small affordances, such as a linter guardrail, a bounded viewer, or a non-empty acknowledgment, are where error recovery starts.

3.3 Anthropic, "Writing Effective Tools for Agents, with Agents" (Sep 2025)

This is the most complete public method for tool design [2]. It frames tools as "a contract between deterministic systems and non-deterministic agents." It has two parts: a process and a set of principles.

Process (evaluation-driven).

  prototype tools --> generate realistic eval tasks --> run agent loop programmatically
        ^             (multi-call, verifiable)          (while-loop; reasoning +
        |                                                feedback blocks)
        |                                                       |
        |                                                       v
  agent refactors tools <-- concatenate transcripts <-- collect metrics: accuracy,
  (Claude Code) and          and failure analysis        runtime, #calls, tokens,
  descriptions                                           tool errors
        |
        +--> validate on held-out test set
  • Tasks should be grounded in realistic workflows that may need dozens of calls. For example, schedule a meeting with a named colleague, attach prior notes, and book a room, rather than "schedule a meeting with x@y.com" [2].
  • Verifiers should not reject correct answers over formatting. Expected tool sequences are optional and should not over-specify the strategy [2].
  • The metrics to collect are accuracy, per-call and per-task runtime, total calls, total tokens, and tool errors. Redundant calls suggest that pagination or consolidation needs fixing. Many invalid-parameter errors suggest that descriptions or examples need fixing [2].
  • One real case: Claude kept appending "2025" to web-search queries, which biased the results. The fix was a better description [2].
  • Anthropic reports that Claude-optimized Slack and Asana MCP servers beat human-written versions on held-out sets. The post shows this as charts without exact figures [2].

Principles.

Principle Concrete guidance [2][8]
Choose tools deliberately Don't wrap every endpoint. Prefer search_contacts to list_contacts.
Consolidate workflows schedule_event instead of list_users + list_events + create_event. get_customer_context instead of three getters. Claude docs suggest one tool with an action parameter over create_pr/review_pr/merge_pr.
Namespace asana_search, jira_search; asana_projects_search. Prefix versus suffix choice affects results and varies by model, so evaluate it.
Return meaningful context Return name, image_url, file_type, not uuid or mime_type. Resolving UUIDs to readable or 0-indexed IDs improved precision.
Offer verbosity control A response_format enum (concise/detailed). In one example, 72 vs 206 tokens. In Slack, concise was about 1/3 the tokens, but detailed returned IDs (thread_ts, channel_id) needed by follow-up calls.
Be token-efficient Pagination, filtering, and truncation with sensible defaults. Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default. A truncation message should steer toward narrower queries.
Make errors actionable Explain what to fix and give an example of correct input, not opaque codes or tracebacks.
Prompt-engineer descriptions Write for a new hire: name specialized formats and resource relationships. Use user_id, not user. Description refinements helped Claude 3.5 Sonnet reach SOTA on SWE-bench Verified.
Annotate MCP tool annotations can flag open-world or destructive tools.

Claude's API documentation adds that detailed descriptions are "by far the most important factor in tool performance." It recommends at least 3-4 sentences per tool, covering what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means, and caveats [8]. The documentation also warns against parameters that ask the model to spell out its step-by-step reasoning. A request for a short explanation or evidence is preferred [8].

The companion context-engineering post names bloated, overlapping toolsets as "one of the most common failure modes," because overlap makes it unclear which tool to use. It argues for a minimal viable toolset that is easier to maintain and prune over long interactions [5].

3.4 Tool Use Examples (Nov 2025)

Problem. JSON Schema states which inputs are valid. It does not show usage conventions such as date formats, ID patterns, which optional parameters appear together, or how to tell create_ticket from create_incident.

Design. An input_examples array on the tool definition. Each example must validate against the schema, and an invalid example returns a 400 error [8]. Examples cost about 20-50 tokens when simple and 100-200 tokens for complex nested objects [8]. Anthropic recommends 1-5 realistic examples (not placeholders like "string"), added only where the schema leaves usage ambiguous [3].

Result. In Anthropic's internal tests on complex parameter handling, accuracy rose from 72% to 90% [3].

3.5 The "think" tool (Mar 2025; superseded Dec 2025)

Anthropic's think tool is a no-op tool whose only purpose is to give the model a scratchpad in the middle of a response, mainly to process new tool results [7]. On tau-bench airline (Claude 3.7 Sonnet), think plus an optimized prompt scored pass^1 0.584, against a 0.332 baseline. The post's text cites a 54% relative improvement over the next-best configuration [7]. On SWE-bench, the isolated gain was about 1.6% on average [7]. Anthropic recommended it for policy-heavy, sequential settings and not for single or parallel non-sequential calls. A December 2025 update says improved extended thinking now makes a dedicated think tool unnecessary in most cases [7]. This is a useful example of a tool-design pattern being absorbed into the model.

4. Tool Selection at Scale

4.1 The two failure modes of "load everything"

  1. Context and cost bloat. In Anthropic's examples, about 55K tokens go to definitions for 58 tools, Jira alone takes about 17K, and one deployment reached 134K before optimization [3].
  2. Selection accuracy. Claude's documentation states that the model's ability to pick the right tool "degrades once you exceed 30-50 available tools" [11]. OpenAI's function-calling guidance, as reproduced in third-party copies, recommends aiming for fewer than 20 functions available at any one time and evaluating performance at different counts [23]. On edge devices, "Less is More" (2024) cut the tools shown per request through recommendation plus similarity search. It reported up to 70% lower execution time and up to 40% lower power use [32].

4.2 Retrieval-based selection: the research line

  • ToolLLM / ToolBench (ICLR 2024). The authors collected 16,464 REST APIs from RapidAPI, grouped into 3,451 tools. They generated instructions and annotated solution paths with DFSDT, a depth-first search decision tree that lets the model evaluate several reasoning paths and backtrack. DFSDT solved instructions that plain CoT or ReAct could not. A neural API retriever recommends APIs per instruction, and the reported pass rate drops only slightly compared with ground-truth API sets [29].
  • ToolRet (ACL Findings 2025). This benchmark has 7.6K retrieval tasks over a corpus of about 43K tools. Its central finding: models that score well on conventional IR benchmarks retrieve tools poorly, and this lowers downstream pass rates. Training on the 200K-instance ToolRet-train set raised tool-use pass rates by 10-20% [30].
  • RAG-MCP (2025). A needle-in-a-haystack stress test presents N MCP schemas (one correct, N-1 distractors). Retrieving and injecting only the best-matching MCP description raised selection accuracy from 13.62% to 43.13% and cut prompt tokens by more than half. Retrieval precision degrades as the registry grows [31].

Lesson. Tool retrieval is its own IR problem. Tool descriptions are short, functional, and full of jargon, so generic embedding retrievers underperform on them. Description quality from Section 3 becomes searchability.

4.3 Anthropic Tool Search Tool (Nov 2025; GA in later docs)

Architecture.

  request.tools = [ tool_search (non-deferred), top 3-5 hot tools (non-deferred),
                    N deferred tools (defer_loading: true, full defs still sent) ]
        |
        v
  context prefix = search tool + hot tools only  (cache-stable)
        |
  model --server_tool_use(pattern|query, limit)--> API-side regex or BM25 search over
        |                                         names, descriptions, arg names/descs
        |<-- tool_search_tool_result { tool_reference[] } (default up to 5)
        |
  API expands references inline into full definitions (appended, prefix untouched)
        |
  model --tool_use(discovered tool)--> client executes --> tool_result

Key properties, from the documentation [11]:

  • Two variants. In the regex variant, the model writes Python re.search patterns (at most 200 characters, case-insensitive). In the BM25 variant, it writes natural-language queries (at most 500 characters).
  • Limits. Up to 10,000 deferred tools per request. At least one tool must stay non-deferred, or the request fails with a 400 error.
  • Caching. Deferred tools are kept out of the system-prompt prefix, and discovered definitions are appended inline. This preserves prompt caching, and discovered tools stay usable in later turns without another search.
  • Custom search. Any client tool can return tool_reference blocks, which enables embedding-based search.
  • MCP. Whole MCP servers can be deferred via mcp_toolset.default_config.

Numbers. The 58-tool example drops from about 77K tokens of overhead to about 8.7K (an 85% reduction). Accuracy on internal MCP evaluations rose from 49% to 74% for Opus 4 and from 79.5% to 88.1% for Opus 4.5 [3].

When not to use it. Fewer than 10 tools, every tool used in every request, or very small definitions [11].

Failure modes. If no description contains the words the model searches for, the right tool cannot be found [11]. Each search adds a round trip. Discovery accuracy now depends on naming and description keywords, and the documentation recommends consistent service prefixes so that one query matches a whole group [11].

4.4 OpenAI tool search and namespaces (2026)

OpenAI's Responses API added a hosted tool_search for GPT-5.4 and later models. Functions, functions inside a namespace, or whole MCP servers can be marked defer_loading: true. When the model needs a deferred tool, the output gains a tool_search_call item and a tool_search_output item that lists the newly callable subset. Newly discovered tools are injected at the end of the context to keep the cache intact [24]. Two vendors arriving at the same design (deferred definitions, appended expansion, cache-preserving prefix) suggests it is becoming the standard answer to toolset scale.

4.5 Progressive disclosure through a filesystem

Anthropic's "Code execution with MCP" (Nov 2025) takes a different approach to discovery. MCP servers are generated into a file tree, ./servers/<server>/<tool>.ts, and each file wraps one MCP call. The agent lists directories and reads only the files it needs. An alternative is a search_tools tool with adjustable detail levels, from name only up to the full schema [4]. Here discovery is ordinary agentic file exploration. This links tool selection to the code-as- action designs in Section 5.

5. Code as the Action Space

5.1 CodeAct (ICML 2024)

Problem. JSON and text actions allow one predefined tool per turn. They cannot compose calls, hold intermediate objects, loop, or branch without a model round trip each time.

Design. Executable Python is the single, unified action space. The agent emits code. A Python interpreter runs it, and stdout, errors, and tracebacks become the next observation. This lets the model use existing libraries and debug itself across multiple turns [14][15].

Results.

  • Across 17 LLMs on API-Bank and the new M3ToolEval benchmark, CodeAct beat Text and JSON actions by up to 20% absolute success rate [14][15].
  • The project also released CodeActInstruct (about 7K multi-turn interactions) and CodeActAgent models fine-tuned from Llama-2-7B (4K context) and Mistral-7B (32K context) [15].
  • smolagents and Hugging Face materials cite the CodeAct line of work as using about 30% fewer steps, and therefore fewer LLM calls, than JSON tool calling [16]. Treat this as approximate.

5.2 smolagents (Hugging Face, Dec 2024 onward)

Architecture. The agent logic fits in about 1,000 lines (agents.py) [16]. Two agent types are offered:

  • CodeAgent (recommended) writes Python snippets in which tools are plain function calls.
  • ToolCallingAgent uses the provider's native JSON tool calling.

Tools can come from MCP servers, LangChain, or Hugging Face Spaces. Agents and tools can be shared on the Hub [16].

Why code? The library gives four reasons [17][20]:

  • Composability: actions nest and can be reused.
  • Object management: an image output can live in a variable.
  • Generality: code can express any computable task.
  • Training-data fit: models have seen far more code than tool-call JSON.

Evidence. In Hugging Face's Open Deep Research replication, a CodeAgent reached 55.15% on the GAIA validation set, against about 46% for the previous best open framework (Magentic-One). Switching the same system to JSON actions dropped it to about 33% [18]. This is one of the cleanest public ablations of code versus JSON actions at system level, although it is measured on the validation split.

Execution security. The built-in LocalPythonExecutor interprets the AST operation by operation. It blocks imports (and submodules) outside an allowlist, raises an error on undefined operations, and caps the number of elementary operations to stop runaway loops [19]. The docs state that "no local python sandbox can ever be completely secure," and give an example: an authorized package like Pillow could still be used to fill a disk. Remote sandboxes are recommended instead: E2B, Modal, Blaxel, or Docker [19]. The hardened Docker example runs as nobody with 512 MB of memory, a 100-process limit, dropped capabilities, and no-new-privileges [19]. A sandbox that covers only code snippets does not support managed multi-agent setups. Sandboxing the whole system may mean putting API keys inside the sandbox [19].

5.3 Anthropic Programmatic Tool Calling (Nov 2025; GA in 2026 docs)

Problem. Every tool result in classic tool calling passes through the model's context. Every dependent call costs another inference pass, typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds each [3].

Architecture.

  model ---writes Python---> [ code_execution container (sandbox) ]
                               |  tools with allowed_callers=[code_execution]
                               |  appear as async functions
                               |
                               |  await query_db({...}) --pause--> API returns tool_use
                               |                                 with caller=code_exec,
                               |                                 container id + expires_at
  client executes tool  <------------------------------------+
  client sends tool_result (tool_result only, same container) +
                               |  code resumes; filter/aggregate/loop/asyncio.gather
                               v
                     only final stdout/result enters model context

Mechanics [12]:

  • Tools opt in through allowed_callers and are exposed as async Python functions that take a dict and return a string.
  • Each tool call pauses execution and surfaces a tool_use block with a caller field, which is how the client tells programmatic calls apart from direct ones.
  • Idle containers are reclaimed after about 5 minutes. A pending tool call times out after about 4 minutes and raises TimeoutError inside the running code, where Claude typically sees it in stderr and retries.
  • Incompatibilities: strict: true tools, forcing programmatic calls through tool_choice, disable_parallel_tool_use, MCP-connector tools, and schemas with recursive $ref.
  • allowed_callers "is not a hard API-level block." Clients must still be ready for direct invocation, and the field must not be treated as a security boundary.

Numbers [3]:

  • Average tokens on complex research tasks fell from 43,588 to 27,297 (-37%).
  • Internal knowledge retrieval accuracy rose from 25.6% to 28.5%, and GIA benchmarks from 46.5% to 51.2%.
  • In a budget-compliance example (20 employees, 2,000+ expense lines), the post describes about 200 KB of raw data reduced to about 1 KB of results. The same post elsewhere describes the raw data as "50 KB+," so treat the magnitude as approximate.
  • Orchestrating 20+ calls in one code block removes 19+ inference passes.

Anthropic recommends it for aggregating large datasets, three or more dependent calls, and fan- out across many items. It recommends against it for single calls or when the model must reason over every intermediate result [3].

Downstream use. In February 2026, Anthropic shipped web search and web fetch tools that dynamically filter results by writing code before results enter context. Across BrowseComp and DeepSearchQA this gave an average 11% improvement with 24% fewer input tokens. For example, Opus 4.6 on BrowseComp rose from 45.3% to 61.6%. Price-weighted cost fell for Sonnet 4.6 but rose for Opus 4.6, because it wrote more code [13][12].

5.4 Code execution with MCP and Cloudflare Code Mode

Anthropic's "Code execution with MCP" (Jones and Kelly, Nov 2025) generalizes the idea to whole MCP ecosystems [4]:

  • Filesystem tool APIs. Tools appear as files (Section 4.5).
  • Context-efficient results. For example, log 5 rows of a 10,000-row sheet.
  • Native control flow.
  • Privacy. Intermediate data stays in the sandbox, and the MCP client can tokenize PII before it reaches the model.
  • State persistence in ./workspace/.
  • Skills. Working code is saved in ./skills/ with a SKILL.md file.
  • Headline example. A Google Drive → Salesforce workflow drops from about 150,000 tokens to about 2,000 (-98.7%).
  • Cost. Secure sandboxing, resource limits, and monitoring add operational overhead that direct tool calls avoid [4].

Cloudflare reached the same conclusion independently. Its September 2025 "Code Mode" post argued that agents should write code against typed APIs instead of calling MCP tools directly. In February 2026 Cloudflare followed up with an MCP server that exposes its entire API through only two tools [21]:

  • search() runs JavaScript against the OpenAPI specification.
  • execute() runs JavaScript against the API inside a Dynamic Worker (V8 isolate) sandbox.

Cloudflare reports that an equivalent non-Code-Mode server would need about 1.17 million tokens of tool definitions, so the two-tool design cuts input tokens by about 99.9% [21]. Secondary coverage describes 2,500+ endpoints served in about 1,000 tokens (approximate) [21].

5.5 Comparison of action-space designs

Design Action unit Round trips per N dependent calls Intermediate data in context Selection mechanism Main risks Reported gains
Prompted ReAct [26] Text "Action:" line N All All tools in prompt Parse errors, hallucinated tools +34 / +10 pts (ALFWorld / WebShop)
Native JSON function calling [8][23] Typed tool-call block N (parallel calls help when independent) All All tools in prompt; tool_choice Bloat; selection degrades past ~30-50 tools [11] Baseline
JSON + tool search [11][24] Typed call after discovery N + searches All Regex/BM25/hosted search over deferred defs Discovery misses if descriptions lack keywords Opus 4 49%→74%; ~85% fewer tokens [3]
CodeAct / smolagents [14][16] Python program ~1 per program Only printed output Tools as functions in prompt Sandbox escape; code bugs Up to +20% SR [14]; GAIA 55% vs 33% JSON [18]
Programmatic Tool Calling [12] Python in managed container calling client tools 1 model pass; N client executions Final output only allowed_callers opt-in Container timeouts; no strict mode -37% tokens; GIA 46.5→51.2% [3]
Code exec with MCP / Code Mode [4][21] TS/JS program against generated SDK ~1 per program Final output only Filesystem or search() over spec Ops overhead; isolation 150K→2K tokens [4]; ~99.9% fewer input tokens [21]
Masked fixed toolset (Manus) [22] Typed call, logit-constrained N All (file system used as memory) State machine masks logits Requires decoder control or prefill KV-cache stability (qualitative)

6. Error Recovery

6.1 Error taxonomy at the protocol layer

Two layers must be kept separate.

  • Protocol errors vs. execution errors (MCP). A malformed or unsupported request returns a JSON-RPC error, which means the tool never ran. A valid request whose execution failed returns a successful JSON-RPC response with isError: true in the result. Only the second kind carries content the model can read and react to [38].
  • Claude client tools. The harness returns a tool_result with is_error: true and an explanatory content field [9]. For invalid calls, such as a missing required parameter, the documentation states that Claude "will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing to the user." It recommends strict: true to eliminate schema violations entirely [9].
  • Server tools (web search, tool search, code execution) report errors inside 200-status result blocks with codes such as too_many_requests, invalid_tool_input, unavailable, and max_uses_exceeded. The model handles these transparently [9][11].

6.2 Error messages as prompts

Several sources agree that the content of an error message is itself a steering prompt:

  • Write "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds.", not "failed" [9].
  • Explain what to fix and show an example of correct input, not opaque codes or raw tracebacks [2].
  • A truncation notice should tell the agent how to narrow its query [2].
  • SWE-agent's linter rejects broken edits before they land. Its explicit "ran successfully and did not produce any output" message stops the model from misreading silence as failure [34].

6.3 Keep the failure in the transcript

The Manus team argues for leaving failed actions and their error observations in the context, instead of cleaning them up or retrying silently, so that the model can learn from them [22]. This principle is reported in secondary summaries of the post as a counterintuitive but central error-recovery practice [22]. CodeAct's design reaches the same point from another direction. Tracebacks are ordinary observations, which is what makes multi-turn self-debugging possible [14]. In Programmatic Tool Calling, a tool TimeoutError appears in the code's stderr, and Claude typically retries [12].

6.4 Verification as a loop stage

The Claude Agent SDK guidance lists three verification mechanisms [6]:

  • Rules-based feedback, such as linters and validators that say which rule failed. The guidance suggests generating TypeScript over JavaScript to gain extra feedback layers.
  • Visual feedback, such as screenshots or renders, for example through Playwright MCP.
  • LLM-as-judge for fuzzy criteria, described as less robust and adding latency and cost.

When the agent keeps failing, the post's prescriptions are about tools: check whether the agent has the right tools, make search APIs easier, add formal rules to tool calls, and offer alternative tools if the agent cannot fix its own errors [6].

6.5 Recovery-relevant protocol edge cases (Claude)

These come from the stop-reasons documentation [10]:

  • Incomplete tool call at max_tokens. If the last block is a truncated tool_use, retry with a higher max_tokens. The partial call is not usable.
  • Empty end_turn. A response of 2-3 tokens with no content, often after tool results, is usually caused by adding text right after tool_result blocks. Do not resend the empty response unchanged. As a last resort, add a new user message such as "Please continue."
  • refusal. Returned with HTTP 200. Read stop_details, and on supported models retry on a fallback model.

7. Stopping Conditions

7.1 Why stopping is a design problem

An agent loop has no natural upper bound. Anthropic notes that tasks usually end on completion, but that "it's also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control" [1]. Public implementations combine several layers of stops:

  +--------------------------- outer budget ---------------------------+
  |  wall-clock / cost / token budget (harness)                         |
  |  +----------------------- turn budget ---------------------------+  |
  |  |  max_turns (OpenAI SDK), max iterations (loop), server-tool    |  |
  |  |  loop cap -> pause_turn (default 10)                           |  |
  |  |  +------------------- semantic stop -----------------------+  |  |
  |  |  |  model ends turn with no tool calls / typed final output |  |  |
  |  |  |  explicit final_answer tool (smolagents)                 |  |  |
  |  |  |  verification passes (tests, linters, judge)             |  |  |
  |  |  +----------------------------------------------------------+  |  |
  |  +----------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  |  context limit -> compaction / tool-result clearing / truncation    |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------+

7.2 Provider stop signals

Signal Provider Meaning Harness action
end_turn Anthropic [10] Model finished Use the output; guard against empty responses
tool_use Anthropic [10] Client tool requested Execute and return a tool_result for every call
pause_turn Anthropic [10] Server-tool sampling loop hit its limit (default 10) Send the assistant content back unchanged; cap continuations
max_tokens Anthropic [10] Output cap hit Raise the cap or continue; discard a partial tool_use
model_context_window_exceeded Anthropic [10] Context filled Treat as truncated; compact
refusal Anthropic [10] Declined (HTTP 200) Read stop_details; fall back to another model
Final output (no tool calls, correct type) OpenAI Agents SDK [25] Semantic completion Return the result
MaxTurnsExceeded OpenAI Agents SDK [25] Turn cap hit (max_turns=None disables it) Raise, or use the max_turns error handler to return a controlled final_output
final_answer tool call smolagents [16][20] Agent declares completion Return its argument

The OpenAI SDK's max_turns error handler is a useful pattern. Instead of failing hard, the run returns a fallback final_output, and include_in_history controls whether that fallback is saved into the session [25]. Developer reports on the OpenAI forum describe MaxTurnsExceeded during tool chaining where partial results could not be recovered [25]. That is an argument for persisting intermediate state outside the transcript.

7.3 Context exhaustion as a stopping (or continuation) condition

Long-horizon agents hit the context limit before they hit a turn cap. Anthropic describes three responses [5]:

  • Compaction: summarize the history near the limit, keeping architectural decisions and open bugs and dropping redundant tool output.
  • Tool-result clearing: drop old raw results, described as "one of the safest, lightest touch forms of compaction."
  • Just-in-time retrieval: keep identifiers such as paths and queries instead of payloads.

Manus uses the file system as externalized memory. Secondary accounts also describe it rewriting a todo.md at each step so that current goals stay at the end of the context [22]. All of these turn a hard stop into a continuation.

7.4 Reliability: stopping correctly, repeatedly

τ-bench (Sierra) evaluates tool-agent-user conversations by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state. It introduced pass^k: the probability that all k independent trials succeed. At release, gpt-4o-class function-calling agents solved fewer than 50% of tasks, and pass^8 in retail was below 25% [36][37]. Sierra reports that τ²-bench added a telecom domain [37]. For loop design, pass^k shows that a loop which usually stops at the right state is not production-ready. Consistency needs tool guardrails, policy reasoning (for example the think tool's τ-bench gains [7]), and deterministic checks.

8. Measuring Function Calling

  • BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard). BFCL describes itself as the first comprehensive and executable function-call evaluation [35]. Its versions:

    • v1: AST-checked simple, parallel, and multiple calls.
    • v2: live, user-contributed functions.
    • v3: multi-turn and multi-step calls. Aggregator descriptions say v3 checks the resulting API state and not only the call format [35].
    • v4: agentic categories (web search, memory management, and format sensitivity) [35].

    Aggregated per-model v4 snapshots show multi-turn accuracy far below single-turn AST accuracy for some small models, for example single digits against 70-87% [35]. These are single-model data points and should not be generalized.

  • τ-bench / τ²-bench. Stateful, policy-constrained, multi-turn conversations with a simulated user, reported as pass^k [36][37].

  • Internal tool evaluations. Anthropic's process in Section 3.3 is the reference method for evaluating your own tools: realistic tasks, verifiable outcomes, a held-out split, and transcripts read by humans and agents [2].

9. Cross-Cutting Comparison: Production Tool-Use Stacks

Capability Anthropic Claude API OpenAI (Responses / Agents SDK) Hugging Face smolagents MCP (protocol)
Tool definition name, description, input_schema, input_examples, strict, defer_loading, allowed_callers [8][11][12] JSON Schema functions, strict, namespaces, defer_loading [23][24] Python functions / Tool classes; MCP, LangChain, Spaces [16] tools/list schemas plus annotations [2][38]
Choice control auto/any/tool/none; forced choice prefills, skips thinking [8] auto/required/none/specific [23] Code or JSON agent type [16] n/a (client decides)
Schema guarantee Strict tool use (grammar) [8] Strict mode / structured outputs [23] Code parsing / interpreter errors n/a

Key Takeaways for System Designers

  1. Treat tool definitions as prompts and the toolset as a product. Description quality is "by far the most important factor" [8]. Ship tool changes only after an evaluation loop with realistic multi-call tasks, verifiable outcomes, and a held-out split [2].
  2. Design tools for workflows, not endpoints. Consolidate (schedule_event, get_customer_context), namespace by service, return human-readable identifiers, and offer a response_format verbosity switch [2][8].
  3. Poka-yoke inputs and use constrained decoding. Require absolute paths, use enums and unambiguous names like user_id, add input_examples for convention-heavy tools (72%→90% [3]), and turn on strict mode to remove schema errors entirely [1][8][9].
  4. Budget the context like a cache-sensitive system. Keep the tool prefix stable. Prefer masking or deferred loading appended at the end over editing definitions mid-task. Measure KV cache hit rate [22][11][24].
  5. Above roughly 10-30 tools, switch to discovery. Keep the 3-5 hot tools loaded and defer the rest behind search (regex, BM25, or embeddings). Be aware that generic retrievers are not "tool-savvy" [11][30][31].
  6. Use code as the action space when calls are dependent, data is large, or work fans out. The evidence is consistent across groups: CodeAct (+20% SR), GAIA (55% vs 33%), PTC (-37% tokens), MCP code execution (-98.7% tokens), and Code Mode (~99.9% fewer definition tokens) [14][18][3][4][21]. Pay for it with real sandboxing. Do not treat an in-process interpreter or allowed_callers as a security boundary [19][12].
  7. Make errors informative, and keep them visible. Return is_error / isError results with remediation hints. Keep failures in the transcript so the model can adapt. Separate protocol failures, where the tool never ran, from execution failures [9][22][38].
  8. Add verification to the loop itself. Use linters, tests, renders, and judges, and give the agent alternative tools when it cannot fix its own errors [6][34].
  9. Layer stopping conditions. Combine the semantic stop (no tool calls, typed final output, final_answer), turn caps with graceful handlers, handling for every provider stop reason (including pause_turn and truncated tool_use), and compaction for context limits [10][25][5].
  10. Optimize for pass^k, not pass@1. Production reliability means repeated success. Many of the techniques above (guardrails, policy reasoning, deterministic tools) matter mainly through consistency [36][7].
  11. Expect techniques to be absorbed into models and platforms. The think tool gave way to better extended thinking [7], and dynamic filtering moved code-based result pruning into first-party search tools [13]. Keep harness abstractions thin enough to drop scaffolding.
