07. Computer and Browser Use Agents: Pixels, Accessibility Trees, and the Race from 15% to Human-Level on OSWorld

Overview

A computer-use agent (CUA) operates software through the same interface a person uses: the screen, the mouse and the keyboard. A browser-use agent does the same inside a web browser. It may also read the page's DOM or accessibility tree. These agents matter because most enterprise software has no API. They also matter because the GUI is the most general action space ever built.

In October 2024, Anthropic shipped the first frontier-model computer use API. It scored 14.9% on OSWorld, against a human baseline of roughly 72% [1][2]. In December 2025, an open agentic framework (Agent S3 with Behavior Best-of-N) claimed 72.6% on OSWorld, which it described as the first result above human level [34]. By September 2026, Anthropic reported 81.8% for Claude Opus 5.5 on the harder, long-horizon OSWorld 2.1, using partial-credit scoring [11]. The benchmark had to be rebuilt twice along the way: as OSWorld-Verified in July 2025, then as OSWorld 2.0/2.1 in 2026 [30][31].

This chapter covers the main designs in that period:

  • Frontier-model, pixel-native CUAs: OpenAI's Computer-Using Agent (Operator, ChatGPT agent and the later GA computer tool), Anthropic's Claude computer use and browser toolsets, and Google's Gemini Computer Use and Project Mariner. Each takes screenshots in and returns coordinate-level actions.
  • Open-source browser frameworks: Browser Use, Stagehand and Skyvern. These wrap a general LLM in a structured view of the DOM or accessibility tree and a deterministic browser driver.
  • Research agents and models: OSWorld, WebArena, WebVoyager, SeeAct, UI-TARS, Agent S, OpenCUA, OmniParser, UFO, Fara and others. These set the benchmarks and the architectural vocabulary: grounding, set-of-marks, planner/actor splits and best-of-N trajectory selection.
  • The cross-cutting question: should an agent perceive the interface as pixels, as an accessibility (a11y) tree or DOM, or as both?
  • The other constant: prompt injection. Every system in this chapter treats it as an open security problem.

A note on sources. This chapter relies on primary documentation, model cards, release notes and source code. During research, some vendor pages (openai.com, deepmind.google, blog.google) could not be retrieved directly. Facts attributed to them are those reported in their announcements, cross-checked against independent primary sources where possible, such as Google's model card, which tabulates OpenAI's CUA results [18]. Figures that could not be cross-checked are marked approximate.

1. The canonical CUA loop

Every system in this chapter is a variation on one loop. Chapter 02 describes the generic agent loop. The CUA version adds three components:

  1. An environment that can render a screen and accept input events: a VM, a container, a headless browser, or the user's own browser.
  2. An observation encoder: a screenshot, an a11y tree, serialized DOM, or a mix.
  3. An action decoder: mapping model output to coordinates, element IDs or code.
   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |                         Agent harness (client side)                      |
   |                                                                          |
   |  task --> [ LLM / VLM ] --tool_use--> [ action executor ] --> environment |
   |              ^   ^                     (xdotool, PyAutoGUI,   (VM / X11 / |
   |              |   |                      Playwright, CDP)       browser)   |
   |              |   +-- history (pruned screenshots, memory, todo)           |
   |              |                                                          |
   |              +------ observation <-- [ encoder ] <-- screen / DOM / AX ---+
   |                      (image, a11y text, SoM overlay, URL, tabs)           |
   |                                                                          |
   |  guards: domain allowlist, confirmation gates, injection classifier,     |
   |          step budget, human takeover                                     |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Anthropic's documentation states the loop plainly [3]:

  1. Send a request with the computer tool.
  2. If stop_reason is tool_use, execute each tool call in order.
  3. Return one tool_result per call: an image for screenshot or zoom, "OK" for other actions.
  4. Repeat until the model emits no tool calls or an iteration cap is hit.

Gemini's reference agent uses the same structure. It retries model calls up to five times with exponential backoff. It treats "no function call" as completion. It returns the current URL alongside each screenshot [19]. OpenAI's Agents SDK runs each batch of actions from a computer_call and replies with a computer_call_output that contains a fresh screenshot [16].

Across vendors, these loops have converged on five design points:

  • Actions are batched. Early APIs emitted one action per turn. By 2026, Anthropic's computer_toolset_20260801 and OpenAI's GA computer tool both return several actions per turn. The harness must run them in order and halt at the first failure [3][16].
  • Coordinates are model-native and must be rescaled. Claude predicts pixel coordinates in the screenshot it was shown. Gemini predicts on a normalized 0-1000 grid that the client maps back to pixels [3][19].
  • Screenshot history is aggressively truncated. Gemini's reference agent keeps images only for the three most recent turns [19]. Anthropic recommends keeping about three screenshots and pruning in batches so the prompt cache prefix stays stable [5].
  • Safety checks travel in-band. OpenAI's pending_safety_checks and Gemini's safety_decision: require_confirmation both come back as fields on a proposed action. The harness must acknowledge them before executing [16][19].
  • Execution stays on the client. Anthropic's computer and browser toolsets are explicitly "client toolsets". Screenshots and inputs stay in the developer's environment, which makes computer use eligible for zero data retention [3][4].

2. Benchmarks: how the field measures itself

Benchmarks shaped CUA architecture more than in most agent subfields, so they are covered before the systems.

2.1 OSWorld and its successors

OSWorld (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2024) put agents in real Ubuntu, Windows and macOS VMs. It used 369 tasks spanning office apps, browsers, IDEs, file managers and multi-app workflows. Each task had an execution-based evaluation script [29][30].

  • Humans completed about 72% of tasks. The best 2024 model baseline completed about 12%.
  • The authors identified GUI grounding and operational knowledge as the main bottlenecks [29].
  • The harness supported several observation types (screenshot, a11y tree, screenshot plus a11y tree, and set-of-marks) and a pyautogui action space. It became the standard testbed for the pixels-versus-structure debate (Section 9).

The benchmark changed four times:

Date Version What changed
2024-04 OSWorld Original 369-task release; VMware and later Docker, AWS and Azure providers [30]
2025-07-28 OSWorld-Verified Community-reported task fixes, AWS parallelism, re-run official results [30]
2026-06-26 OSWorld 2.0 Long-horizon, real-world tasks; mocked websites and self-hosted GitLab [31]
2026-09-16 OSWorld 2.1 Bug-fix release with pinned task, asset, website and image references; recommended [31]

Three design choices make OSWorld scores hard to game:

  • Step limits. Results are reported at 15, 50 or 100 steps. More steps materially raise scores. Claude 3.5 Sonnet went from 14.9% to 22.0% with more steps [1].
  • Maintainer-run verification. Leaderboard entries are verified only after the maintainers run the agent themselves. Submitters must agree to disclose the agent implementation and file a report [30][31].
  • Version boundaries. Anthropic notes that its scores before Sonnet 4.5 used the original OSWorld and its later scores use OSWorld-Verified, so the two are not directly comparable [10].

2.2 Web benchmarks

  • WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023) self-hosts realistic sites: shopping, a shopping admin CMS, Reddit, GitLab, maps and Wikipedia. It has 812 tasks with functional checkers. Its default observation is the accessibility tree [43]. The original paper reported about 14% success for GPT-4 versus about 78% for humans.
  • WebVoyager (He et al., ACL 2024) runs 643 tasks on 15 live websites. It uses screenshots overlaid with bounding boxes around interactive elements (a set-of-marks style) and a GPT-4V judge that reads the last k screenshots [40]. Most 2025 vendor claims use this benchmark: Browser Use, Skyvern 2.0, Mariner, OpenAI CUA and Gemini.
  • Online-Mind2Web (Xue et al., COLM 2025) responded to WebVoyager saturation. It has 300 tasks on 136 live sites, with stale tasks periodically replaced. Its judge, WebJudge, identifies key task points, selects key screenshots, and then judges. It agrees with human labels 85.7% of the time with o4-mini, against 78.7% for the WebVoyager-style judge on the same backbone [41]. The paper's title, "An Illusion of Progress?", captures its argument: live-web benchmarks with lenient automatic judges had overstated agent progress.
  • BrowserGym/AgentLab (ServiceNow) unifies MiniWoB, WebArena, VisualWebArena, WorkArena, AssistantBench and others behind one Gym interface. The WebArena authors themselves recommend it for parallel, reproducible runs [43][44].

Lesson. CUA benchmarks degrade quickly. Live sites change, CAPTCHAs appear, and judges are lenient. Every major benchmark has needed a "verified" or v2 release within about a year. Treat any single number as specific to its harness. Google's own model card lists separate "official leaderboard" and "measured by Browserbase" columns for the same models, and the numbers differ by up to roughly 9 points [18].

3. OpenAI: Computer-Using Agent, Operator, ChatGPT agent

3.1 Problem and architecture

OpenAI introduced the Computer-Using Agent (CUA) model and the Operator product in January 2025 [13][14]. CUA combined GPT-4o's vision with reasoning trained through reinforcement learning. It operated purely on raw screenshots and emitted mouse and keyboard actions, with no DOM or OS APIs. OpenAI framed the loop as perception (a screenshot added to context), reasoning (chain of thought over current and past screenshots) and action (click, scroll, type), repeated until the task is done or user input is needed [13].

Reported launch results were [13][18]:

  • OSWorld: 38.1%
  • WebArena: about 58% (approximate)
  • WebVoyager: 87%

Google's later model card independently tabulates CUA at 38.1% on OSWorld and 87.0% on WebVoyager, and Operator at 61.3% on the official Online-Mind2Web leaderboard [18]. ByteDance's UI-TARS-1.5 comparison reports 36.4% for OpenAI CUA on OSWorld at 100 steps, and 23.4% on the ScreenSpot-Pro grounding benchmark [35]. On the stricter OSWorld-Verified, OpenCUA lists OpenAI CUA at 31.4% at 100 steps [32].

3.2 Operator: product-level safety design

Operator ran CUA in a cloud-hosted browser that the user could watch. OpenAI's announcements and system card described a layered safety design [14]:

  • Takeover mode: the user types credentials and payment details directly, so the model never sees them.
  • User confirmations before consequential actions such as submitting orders or sending email.
  • Task refusals for disallowed categories.
  • Watch mode on sensitive sites, where the agent pauses if the user is inactive.
  • A prompt-injection monitor that halts the agent when on-screen content looks like an attempt to redirect it.

The same layers (handoff of secrets, confirmation gates, category blocks, injection monitors) reappear at Anthropic and Google.

3.3 ChatGPT agent (mid-2025)

In July 2025, OpenAI folded Operator into ChatGPT agent [15]. One agent ran on a virtual computer and combined three things:

  • Operator's visual browser.
  • Deep research's text-based browser, for fast reading and synthesis.
  • A terminal, plus API and connector access.

The architectural point is that pixel-level browsing is expensive and slow. A production agent should choose per step between a text browser, a visual browser, code, and direct API calls. That idea recurs throughout this chapter. Treat any benchmark figure from that announcement not reproduced here as approximate.

3.4 The API surface and its evolution

The developer API began as the computer-use-preview model and computer_use_preview tool in the Responses API. The tool required:

  • an environment and a display size;
  • one action per computer_call;
  • truncation="auto" [16].

By 2026, the OpenAI Agents SDK documents a GA path [16]:

  • computer-use-preview maps to gpt-5.6-sol.
  • The selector becomes computer.
  • computer_call carries batched actions[].
  • Truncation no longer needs to be set.
  • The SDK default model (gpt-5.6-luna) supports computer use.

Safety checks remain in-band. A computer_call may carry pending_safety_checks, and the harness's on_safety_check callback must acknowledge each one. If no callback is set, the SDK proceeds without prompting a person. The documentation therefore tells developers to enforce any must-apply policy inside their own harness [16].

The AsyncComputer interface shows the minimal action set a harness must implement [16]:

  • screenshot
  • click, double_click, move, drag(path)
  • scroll
  • type, keypress
  • wait

OpenAI's current sample app shows a different design. Instead of discrete click actions, the model calls a single exec_py function [17]:

  • It writes Python that uses PyAutoGUI against a persistent interpreter.
  • Screenshots come back as input_image items.
  • Each code call has a 60-second deadline.
  • The runner refuses to start new runs if held input cannot be released.

This code-as-action CUA pattern trades a small, safe action space for expressiveness and fewer round trips. The README warns that generated code runs with the user's permissions and no OS sandbox [17].

Simular reports that OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol scores 62.57% on the 108-task OSWorld 2.0, citing OpenAI's own report [34]. This is approximate and secondhand.

4. Anthropic: Claude computer use, the browser toolset, and Claude in Chrome

4.1 Origin and training lessons

Anthropic released computer use in public beta with the upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet on October 22, 2024. It scored 14.9% on OSWorld's screenshot-only category, against 7.7-7.8% for the next best system, and 22.0% with more steps [1][2]. Early adopters included Asana, Canva, Cognition, DoorDash, Replit and The Browser Company. Replit used the feature to evaluate apps as Replit Agent built them [1].

The engineering post "Developing a computer use model" gives rare detail on training [2]:

  • Pixel counting was the key skill. The model had to count pixels vertically and horizontally to place the cursor accurately. Anthropic called this "critical".
  • Generalization from small worlds. Training used only a few simple programs, such as a calculator and a text editor, with internet access disabled for safety. The model nonetheless generalized and began to self-correct.
  • Known weaknesses at launch. The model was slow and error-prone. Dragging and zooming were hard. The "flipbook" of screenshots could miss short-lived notifications.
  • Prompt injection was flagged on day one as the central risk, because instructions can hide in screenshots of web content. Anthropic added classifiers and steered the model away from social media posting, domain registration and government websites [2].

4.2 The reference architecture

Anthropic's computer-use-demo is the canonical self-hosted setup [6]:

  +---------------------------- Docker container ---------------------------+
  |                                                                          |
  |   X11 virtual display (desktop apps, Firefox)                            |
  |        ^ xdotool / screenshot                                            |
  |        |                                                                 |
  |   tools: computer | bash | str_replace_based_edit_tool                   |
  |        ^                                                                 |
  |        | tool_use / tool_result                                          |
  |   agent loop  <---- Claude API (or Bedrock / Vertex) ---->               |
  |        |                                                                 |
  |   Streamlit chat UI :8501   noVNC :6080   VNC :5900   combined :8080     |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Two design features stand out:

  • Shell and editor tools sit next to the GUI tool. Many steps are cheaper as shell commands or file edits than as clicks.
  • The weak separation is called out explicitly. The agent loop runs inside the container it controls, supports one session at a time, and must be reset between sessions [6].

The demo recommends XGA (1024x768). It scales larger displays down and pads smaller ones, because relying on API-side resizing hurts accuracy and speed [6].

4.3 The 2026 computer toolset

By August 2026, computer_toolset_20260801 replaced the single computer tool, which took an action parameter, with 17 member tools [3]:

  • Capture: screenshot; zoom, which takes a region and returns it at full resolution while coordinates stay in full-screen space.
  • Clicks: left, right, middle, double and triple click.
  • Drags: left_click_drag, plus left_mouse_down and left_mouse_up for fine control.
  • Pointer: mouse_move, cursor_position.
  • Scrolling: scroll.
  • Keyboard: type, key (with a repeat count), hold_key.
  • Timing: wait.

The toolset changes the harness contract in several ways:

  • Batched tool calls are standard. Harnesses run them in order and answer any blocks after a failure with a fixed "Not executed" error [3].
  • The API no longer downscales images; oversized screenshots are rejected. Opus 4.7 and later models accept up to 2576 px on the long edge and about 3.75 MP (4,784 visual tokens). Earlier models accept 1568 px and about 1.15 MP. Clients must resize screenshots and rescale the returned coordinates [3][5].
  • Declaring the toolset costs about 4,500 input tokens; disabling zoom saves about 410. Each screenshot costs about 1,000-1,800 tokens [3].
  • Earlier versions remain available behind beta headers: computer_20250124 and computer_20251124 [3].

Anthropic's published "best practices" (May 2026) give benchmarked guidance that generalizes beyond Claude [5]:

  • Resolution budget. 1280x720 uses about 80% of the 4.6-family pixel budget. A 16 px checkbox on a 4K display shrinks to about 5 px at 1280x720. Avoid going below 960x540. Start Opus 4.7 at 1080p.
  • Thinking effort. For Opus 4.7, high gets close to peak task success at about half the output tokens of max. max adds no accuracy for computer use. Opus 4.7 at low roughly matches Sonnet 4.6 at max with about one-tenth the tokens per task.
  • Context. A 200k window fills in under 100 screenshots. Keep the last 3, prune in batches of 25, place four cache breakpoints (one on the stable prefix, three on recent tool results), and compact at about 150k tokens. Cache hits cost 10% of the input price.
  • Click precision. Sonnet 4.6 had fewer near-misses than Opus 4.6, so a larger model is not always a better clicker.
  • Injection classifiers run in parallel with inference, adding "approximately zero" latency and no cost [5].

4.4 The browser toolset: a hybrid a11y-and-pixel design

For tasks that stay in the browser, Anthropic ships browser_toolset_20260801, with 31 member tools (27 on by default) [4]:

  • Navigation and capture: navigate, screenshot, zoom.
  • Pointer and keyboard: the same family as the computer toolset, plus hover and scroll_to.
  • Page reading: read_page, find, get_page_text.
  • Forms: form_input; file_upload is opt-in.
  • Diagnostics and scripting (opt-in): read_console, read_network, javascript_exec.
  • Tabs: new_tab, list_tabs, switch_tab, close_tab.

The key design decision is that the accessibility tree is the primary observation. read_page returns a11y text with element references such as [ref_2], capped at 50,000 characters. Click, hover and form_input can target a reference instead of a coordinate, "so it doesn't have to locate elements in a screenshot" [4]. find takes a natural-language query and returns up to 20 matching references. Screenshots and zoom remain available for visual verification.

The documentation's security list doubles as a threat model [4]:

  • Run in a fresh, low-privilege profile.
  • Enforce domain allowlists at the network layer and re-check them after redirects.
  • Accept only http(s) URLs, and parse them rather than prefix-matching.
  • Treat titles, URLs and download names as untrusted.
  • Keep javascript_exec and file_upload off unless the task needs them.

Browser Use reports implementing all 31 actions against local, cloud or remote CDP browsers [22].

4.5 Claude in Chrome and injection defense

The Claude in Chrome research preview (August 25, 2025) gave unusually concrete red-team numbers [7]:

  • 123 adversarial test cases across 29 attack scenarios.
  • Attack success rate in autonomous mode: 23.6% without mitigations, 11.2% with them.
  • On four browser-specific attack types, such as hidden DOM fields and URL or tab-title injection: 35.7% without mitigations, 0% with them.

The product mitigations were:

  • per-site permissions;
  • confirmations before publishing, purchasing or sharing personal data;
  • default blocks on financial services, adult and pirated-content sites.

The extension reached Max users in November 2025 and Pro, Team and Enterprise users in December 2025 [7].

Anthropic's November 2025 research post describes three defense layers [8]:

  1. Reinforcement learning on simulated injected web content, rewarding the model for spotting and refusing injections.
  2. Classifiers that scan all untrusted content entering the context: hidden text, manipulated images and deceptive UI.
  3. Continuous human red teaming, including external arena-style challenges run by Gray Swan.

Robustness was measured against an adaptive "Best-of-N" attacker with 100 attempts per environment. The post states that even 1% attack success is "meaningful risk" and that the problem is "far from a solved problem" [8].

4.6 Capability trajectory

Model (date) OSWorld variant Reported score
Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) OSWorld, screenshot-only 14.9% (22.0% with more steps) [1]
Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Feb 2025) OSWorld-Verified, 100 steps (third party) 35.9% [32]
Claude Sonnet 4 (May 2025) OSWorld 42.2% [9]
Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Sep 2025) OSWorld-Verified 61.4% [9]
Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Sep 2026) OSWorld 2.1, partial scoring 80.1% [12]
Claude Opus 5.5 (Sep 2026) OSWorld 2.1, partial scoring 81.8% [11]

Sonnet 4.5 was also reported to stay focused for "more than 30 hours" on multi-step tasks [9]. Sonnet 4.6 (February 2026) reported "human-level capability" on tasks such as complex spreadsheets and multi-step forms. It also improved prompt-injection resistance over Sonnet 4.5, though Anthropic said it still trails the most skilled humans [10]. Note that the 2026 scores use a different benchmark (OSWorld 2.1) and partial-credit scoring, so they cannot be compared directly with the 2024-2025 numbers.

5. Google: Project Mariner and the Gemini Computer Use model

5.1 Project Mariner

Google DeepMind announced Project Mariner in December 2024 as a Gemini 2.0 research prototype running as a Chrome extension [20][21]:

  • It reasoned over the active tab's pixels and web elements: text, code, images and forms.
  • It reported 83.5% on WebVoyager "as a single agent setup".
  • It acted only in the active tab.
  • It asked for confirmation before sensitive actions such as purchases.

Later updates moved Mariner to cloud-hosted VMs that run several tasks in parallel. They also added a "teach and repeat" mode, in which the agent learns a workflow from one demonstration, and fed these capabilities into the Gemini API and the Gemini app's agent mode [21]. The details come from Google's announcements and are not independently verified here.

5.2 Gemini 2.5 Computer Use

The Gemini 2.5 Computer Use model card (October 7, 2025) is the most detailed primary source on Google's design [18]:

  • Base model. Gemini 2.5 Pro (06-2025) with additional post-training for UI control.
  • Scope. Optimized for web browsers. It is not yet optimized for OS-level control, but it "demonstrates promise" on mobile.
  • Interface. Inputs are the task, screenshots and recent action history. Output is a single function call proposing the next action.

Reported results [18]:

Benchmark (source) Gemini 2.5 CU Comparators (as tabulated)
Online-Mind2Web (official leaderboard) 69.0% OpenAI Operator 61.3%
Online-Mind2Web (measured by Browserbase) 65.7% Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 4 and OpenAI CUA lower (approx.)
WebVoyager (official / self-reported) 88.9% OpenAI CUA 87.0%
WebVoyager (measured by Browserbase) 79.9% others about 61-71% (approx.)
AndroidWorld (Google DeepMind) 69.7% Claude Sonnet 4.5 56.0%, Sonnet 4 62.1%
OSWorld not supported Sonnet 4.5 61.4%, Sonnet 4 42.2%, OpenAI CUA 38.1%

Safety is split between the model and an inference-time service [18]:

  • Post-training. The model learns to recognize high-stakes actions (purchases, downloads, sending messages) and to follow developer system instructions that require confirmation.
  • Per-step monitor. A safety service inspects every proposed action. It blocks actions prohibited by policy, forces user confirmation for high-stakes actions, and blocks known dangerous sites.
  • Terms of service forbid developers from bypassing required confirmations.

5.3 The reference harness

Google's computer-use-preview repository adds client-side details [19]:

  • The ComputerUse tool is configured with environment=ENVIRONMENT_BROWSER and an optional list of excluded actions. Developer function declarations can sit next to it.
  • Older models use a legacy action vocabulary: click_at, type_text_at, scroll_document, wait_5_seconds, key_combination. Newer Gemini 3.x models use click, type, scroll, wait, hotkey, press_key.
  • Coordinates arrive on a 0-1000 grid and are mapped to pixels as x/1000*width.
  • A safety_decision with require_confirmation prompts the user. Approval is echoed back as safety_acknowledgement: "true" in the function response.
  • Only the three most recent turns keep screenshots.

By late 2026 the repository's default model was gemini-3.6-flash, and computer use was also supported on gemini-3.5-flash-lite. This is a sign that computer use has moved from a specialized model into general Flash-tier models [19].

A known failure mode: Playwright cannot capture OS-rendered <select> dropdowns on some platforms, so the model sees a wrong screenshot. The suggested fixes are a hosted browser such as Browserbase or injecting a custom-select shim [19]. This is a concrete example of the renderer and screenshot mismatches that pixel-only agents must cope with.

6. Browser Use: DOM-first, LLM-agnostic

6.1 Problem and positioning

Browser Use is an MIT-licensed Python (and TypeScript) library. It lets any LLM drive Chromium. It is among the most-starred agent projects, with about 118k GitHub stars by late 2026 [22]. The project now spans three products [22]:

  • the open library;
  • a hosted cloud with stealth browsers at about $0.02 per browser-hour, CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies;
  • its own browser-optimized model, BU 2.0 (bu-2-0), plus an internal "BU Bench V2" of hard tasks.

6.2 Observation pipeline (from source)

Browser Use's core contribution is a carefully engineered DOM serialization. It does not ask the model to ground actions in pixels. The DomService builds an enhanced tree from four concurrent Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) calls, with a 10 s timeout and a 2 s retry [23]:

  DOMSnapshot.captureSnapshot ---(styles, paint order, rects)---+
  DOM.getDocument(depth=-1, pierce=true) --(shadow roots, iframes)+--> EnhancedDOMTreeNode
  Accessibility.getFullAXTree (per frame) --(roles, names, values)+       |
  Page.getLayoutMetrics ------------------(device pixel ratio)---+       v
                                                         DOMTreeSerializer
     + JS click-listener scan (capped at 100, skipped above 10k elements)  |
                                                                         v
        "[12]<button aria-label=Search />   *[13]<input placeholder=... />"

The serializer applies a series of compression and safety heuristics [24]:

  • Indexing. Only visible, interactive elements get [index] tags. Elements new since the last step are marked with *.
  • Occlusion. Paint-order filtering drops elements covered by others, such as modals and sticky headers.
  • Deduplication. Bounding-box propagation removes descendants that sit 99% or more inside a clickable parent such as an <a> or <button>.
  • Containers. Shadow DOM, iframes and scroll containers are labeled.
  • Compact controls. Selects, sliders, file inputs and media get one-line "compound component" summaries.
  • Size limits. SVGs are collapsed and attribute values are capped at 100 characters.
  • Privacy. Password values are always stripped so they "must not leak into DOM snapshots sent to the LLM".

6.3 Agent loop and prompt contract

The system prompt defines a structured state block [25]:

  • <user_request>
  • <agent_history>
  • <agent_state>, with file-system and todo summaries
  • <browser_state>: URL, tabs and indexed elements
  • <browser_vision>: a screenshot with bounding boxes, treated as ground truth when present
  • <read_state>

The model returns JSON with thinking, evaluation_previous_goal, memory, next_goal, an optional plan update, and a non-empty action list.

Two rules carry most of the reliability engineering:

  • Multi-action steps with page-change barriers. Several actions can be chained per step, but page-changing actions such as navigate, go_back or switch must come last. The runtime also skips the remaining actions if a click unexpectedly navigates [25].
  • A strict done contract. done must be the only action in its step. success=true is allowed only after the agent has verified every requirement against tool output. Long tasks keep a todo.md and results.md on a persistent file system; tasks under about 10 steps should not [25].

Lesson. Browser Use shows that a general LLM with a high-quality, compact, change-annotated DOM view, plus pixels as a secondary signal, can compete with pixel-native CUAs on web tasks. Most of the engineering lives in the serializer, not the model.

7. Stagehand: AI primitives inside deterministic automation

Stagehand (Browserbase) takes the opposite stance to autonomous agents. It is an SDK (TypeScript, Python and Go; v4 by 2026) that adds a few AI primitives to Playwright-style code [26]:

  • act("click the sign-in button") performs a natural-language action.
  • observe(...) returns real selectors for described elements. These can be passed to ordinary locators, so the model never sees the credentials typed into them.
  • extract(schema) returns schema-validated data, using Zod in TypeScript or Pydantic in Python.

The design principle is use AI only where the page is unknown or changing; use code everywhere else. Supporting mechanisms include [26]:

  • hybrid accessibility-tree trimming, so each call sends only the needed page context;
  • self-healing, where act, observe and extract re-derive how an action happens when the site changes;
  • server-side caching (cache: true on Browserbase), so repeated identical calls cost no tokens;
  • a Model Gateway that picks a model per action;
  • a hosted MCP server exposing navigate, act, observe and extract;
  • WebMCP support, so the agent can call tools that pages expose directly.

Browserbase claims 2x faster execution than Playwright-cloud-equivalent browsers but gives no method [26].

Browserbase also matters as infrastructure. Google's reference CUA uses it as a backend, and Google's model card cites Browserbase as an independent evaluator of CUA models [18][19]. That shows a split between the agent "brain" and the remote browser "hands".

8. Skyvern: planner, actor, validator, then compiled scripts

Skyvern (AGPL-3.0 core plus a managed cloud) targets form-heavy business workflows. Its README says it uses "a swarm of agents to comprehend a website, and plan and execute its actions", relying on vision LLMs instead of brittle XPaths [27]. Its reported results [27]:

  • 64.4% on WebBench, where it is strongest on WRITE tasks (forms, logins, downloads);
  • 85.8% on WebVoyager, the figure in the Skyvern 2.0 report title.

Skyvern's open prompt library shows how the swarm is structured [28]:

  user goal
     |
     v
  task_v2 planner ---> mini-goal {navigate | extract | loop | compute}
     ^                     |
     |                     v
  check-user-goal     extract-action actor: screenshot + element tree with IDs
  (validator)              -> [CLICK | INPUT_TEXT | SELECT_OPTION | UPLOAD_FILE |
     ^                         SOLVE_CAPTCHA | COMPLETE | TERMINATE ...] + confidence
     |                     |
     +---- results <-------+
                           |
          script-generation / script-reviewer --> reusable Playwright-style code
          script-failure-triage, cua-fallback-action (fall back to a CUA model)
  • The planner (task_v2) breaks the goal into self-contained mini-goals. Each ends with a success condition and fits the step budget. Loops are preferred for repeated work. A required_subgoals checklist with evidence controls completion. Termination is reserved for explicit "impossible" signals, not CAPTCHAs or empty results [28].
  • The actor (extract-action) sees the clickable element tree and, optionally, a screenshot. It returns JSON actions with per-action reasoning and a confidence_float. It must never invent element IDs and must treat page content as untrusted data even when it claims to be a system message. It should solve CAPTCHAs only after filling the form, because tokens expire [28].
  • Validators (check-user-goal, decisive-criterion-validate, quality-audit) confirm completion.
  • Script generation and review prompts, plus a cua-fallback-action and a UI-TARS system prompt, point to a hybrid strategy. An LLM explores a workflow once, the result is compiled into deterministic code, and an agent (or a CUA model) is called again only on failure [28].

Skyvern also ships the operational features enterprise automation needs [27]:

  • 2FA via TOTP, email and SMS;
  • Bitwarden and custom credential services;
  • livestreamed sessions for human intervention;
  • CDP connection to a local Chrome;
  • workflow blocks (loops, file parsing, HTTP, email);
  • MCP support.

9. Pixels vs. accessibility tree vs. DOM: the central design choice

Dimension Pixels only A11y tree / DOM only Hybrid (both)
Representative systems OpenAI CUA, Gemini CU, Claude computer tool, UI-TARS, Fara WebArena baselines, Agent-E, early Browser Use, Stagehand observe Claude browser toolset, Browser Use (DOM + vision), Skyvern, UFO2, SeeAct-SoM
Generality Any app, OS, canvas, game or remote desktop Web pages, or native apps with good a11y APIs Web and instrumented desktops
Grounding Model must predict coordinates; needs pixel-level skill [2] Exact element IDs; no coordinate error IDs where available, pixels as fallback
Token cost per step About 1,000-1,800 tokens per screenshot [3] Can be large; capped (e.g. 50k chars) [4] Both, unless trimmed
Failure modes Small targets, high-DPI scaling, OS-drawn widgets [5][19] Missing or wrong ARIA, canvas UIs, shadow DOM, iframes, hidden elements Mismatch between the two views
Injection surface Rendered text and images Hidden DOM text, attributes, tab titles [7] Both
Privacy controls Hard to redact pixels Can strip passwords pre-LLM [24] Strip in text; mask in images

The evidence over time:

  1. 2023-2024: structure won. WebArena's default was the accessibility tree [43]. OSWorld's early baselines found that text a11y input beat raw screenshots for general VLMs, and named grounding as the bottleneck [29]. SeeAct separated action generation from grounding and made set-of-marks overlays its default grounding mode [42]. WebVoyager drew boxes around interactive elements on the screenshot [40]. OmniParser parsed screenshots into labeled elements: a YOLO-based detector plus a Florence captioner. That turned pixels into structure for agents that could not ground directly. Its v2 reached 39.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro [36].
  2. 2025: pixel-native models caught up. RL-trained CUAs (OpenAI CUA, Claude, UI-TARS) grounded directly in pixels. UI-TARS-1.5 reached 61.6% on ScreenSpot-Pro, where OpenAI CUA scored 23.4% and Claude 3.7 scored 27.7% [35]. Dedicated grounding data scaled: OSWorld-G and the Jedi dataset (about 4M examples), and OpenCUA's AgentNet with 22.6k human desktop-task demonstrations across three OSes and more than 200 applications [32][33].
  3. 2026: hybrid by default for the browser, pixels for the desktop. Anthropic's browser toolset makes the a11y tree primary and keeps screenshot and zoom for verification [4]. Browser Use treats the screenshot as "ground truth" next to its DOM index [25]. Microsoft's UFO2 uses hybrid UIA-plus-vision control detection on Windows [37]. Whole-desktop agents (Claude's computer toolset, Agent S3, OSWorld entrants) remain mostly pixel-based, with zoom to recover detail [3][34].

The practical rule:

  • Use structure wherever a trustworthy structure exists. It is cheaper, more precise and easier to redact.
  • Use pixels for coverage, for verification ("did the click actually work?"), and for everything structure misses: canvas, remote desktops, games and badly labeled apps.

10. Research architectures that shaped production

10.1 Native agent models: UI-TARS and Fara

UI-TARS (ByteDance, 2025) is an end-to-end "native" GUI agent model. Perception, reasoning, grounding and action all happen in one VLM, with prompt templates for desktop, mobile and grounding-only use. UI-TARS-1.5 adds RL-trained "think before act" reasoning [35]. Reported results for UI-TARS-1.5 [35]:

  • OSWorld (100 steps): 42.5%
  • Windows Agent Arena: 42.1%
  • WebVoyager: 84.8%
  • Online-Mind2Web: 75.8%
  • AndroidWorld: 64.2%

The open 7B release reached 27.5% on OSWorld. UI-TARS-2 (September 2025) extends the approach to games, code and tool use [35].

Fara-7B (Microsoft, 2025) is a small screenshot-only web agent [39]:

  • WebVoyager: 73.5%
  • Online-Mind2Web: 34.1%

Its successor Fara1.5 explicitly avoids accessibility trees and separate parsing models [39]. Microsoft's Magentic-UI 0.2 pairs an on-device orchestrator (MagenticBrain) with Fara as the browser model. Browser sessions run in a lightweight VM sandbox (Quicksand), and users can steer, approve or take over at any point [38].

10.2 Compositional frameworks: Agent S and best-of-N

Simular's Agent S line takes a compositional approach [34]:

  • a generalist planner model (for example, GPT-5);
  • a specialist grounding model (UI-TARS-1.5-7B recommended) that maps described targets to coordinates through an agent-computer interface;
  • an optional reflection agent;
  • a code agent that runs Python and Bash, with a 30 s timeout per Bash script;
  • a trajectory window that keeps 8 image turns by default.

The key result is Behavior Best-of-N (bBoN): run several full rollouts and have a judge pick the best trajectory. Reported gains [34]:

Benchmark Single rollout With bBoN
OSWorld (100 steps) 66% 72.6% (Dec 2025)
WindowsAgentArena (3 rollouts) 50.2% 56.6%
AndroidWorld 68.1% 71.6%

Simular's hosted agent, Sai, reportedly scored 73% on the 108-task OSWorld 2.0 (August 2026) [34].

Lesson. For GUI tasks, test-time compute spent on whole trajectories plus a selector is as effective as spending it inside a single trajectory. This only works when environments can be snapshotted or replicated, so rollouts do not interfere with each other.

10.3 Open data and models: OpenCUA

OpenCUA (XLANG Lab, NeurIPS 2025 spotlight) open-sourced the full stack [32]:

  • an annotation tool that records screen video, input events and a11y trees;
  • the 22.6k-task AgentNet dataset;
  • an offline benchmark;
  • models trained with "reflective long chain-of-thought" that comments on the previous action, the alternatives and the expected next state.

OpenCUA-72B reached 45.0% on OSWorld-Verified at 100 steps. On the same table, Claude 4 Sonnet scored 41.5% and OpenAI CUA 31.4% [32]. XLANG has since released CUA-Gym, a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable training tasks, and CUA-Gym-Hub, a set of mock web apps packaged as RL environments. Synthetic verifiable environments have become the training substrate for the field [31].

10.4 Windows-native: UFO

Microsoft's UFO2 ("Desktop AgentOS", April 2025) uses [37]:

  • a HostAgent that coordinates per-application AppAgents;
  • hybrid UIA-plus-vision control detection;
  • mixed GUI and API actions with deep Win32 and COM integration;
  • RAG over documents and past traces;
  • speculative multi-action execution, which batches predicted actions and reports 51% fewer LLM calls.

UFO3 Galaxy (November 2025) generalizes this to multi-device DAG orchestration [37].

10.5 Hierarchical web agents: Agent-E

Agent-E (Emergence AI, 2024) used a planner over a browser-navigation agent. It introduced DOM distillation modes: text_only for reading, input_fields for acting and all_fields for both, so each step sees the smallest view sufficient for its purpose. It also used mutation observers to verify that actions took effect [45]. Browser Use and Stagehand later adopted the same ideas in their own forms: task-dependent views and change-aware observation.

11. Cross-system comparison

System Perception Action space Planner split Runs where Notable public numbers

12. Failure modes observed across systems

  1. Grounding misses. These are clicks a few pixels off, especially on small targets, at high DPI, or after unaccounted rescaling. The fixes are client-side resizing with coordinate rescaling, zoom actions, specialized grounding models, or a11y references [3][5][34].
  2. Stale or mismatched observations. Examples include OS-rendered dropdowns missing from headless screenshots, content changing between screenshot and click, and brief notifications missed by "flipbook" observation [2][19]. Fixes include * new-element markers, page-change barriers that cut action batches short, and waits [24][25].
  3. Premature or false success. The agent declares the task done without verifying it. This is why Browser Use's done requires evidence [25], Skyvern has validator prompts and evidence-backed subgoals [28], and Online-Mind2Web built a stricter judge [41].
  4. Overly early termination. Agents give up on CAPTCHAs, loading states or empty results. Skyvern's planner explicitly forbids treating these as impossibility [28].
  5. Context exhaustion. Screenshots fill 200k tokens in under 100 steps. The fix is screenshot pruning aligned with cache breakpoints, compaction, and file-based memory (todo.md) [5][25].
  6. Prompt injection. Hidden DOM text, tab titles, URLs and images can redirect the agent. Unmitigated browser attacks succeeded 23.6% of the time in Anthropic's tests. Even with defenses, no vendor claims immunity [7][8].
  7. Irreversible actions. These include purchases, messages, file deletion and accepting terms. Every vendor routes them through confirmations: in-band safety checks [16][19], product gates [7][14], or developer-enforced harness policy [3][4].
  8. Bot detection and authentication friction. CAPTCHAs, 2FA and fingerprinting push production systems toward managed browsers with proxies and solvers, credential-vault integrations, and human takeover [22][27].
  9. Harness side effects. A code-driven CUA can leave keys held down. An in-container loop can be damaged by the agent it controls. Sample apps add failsafes and refuse to start new runs until held input is released [6][17].

13. Cost and latency

Public numbers are sparse, but some anchor points exist:

  • Token cost per step. A Claude screenshot costs about 1,000-1,800 input tokens. Declaring the toolset costs about 4,500 tokens once per request, mostly cacheable [3]. Older tool versions added 466-499 system-prompt tokens plus about 735 tokens per tool definition [3].
  • Thinking budget. Lower effort settings can cut output tokens by 2-10x with little loss in accuracy (Section 4.3) [5].
  • Infrastructure. Browser Use Cloud lists about $0.02 per browser-hour [22]. Skyvern and Browserbase sell anti-bot proxies and solvers as managed add-ons [26][27].
  • Calls per task. UFO2's speculative multi-action cut LLM calls by 51% [37]. Batched actions in the 2026 OpenAI and Anthropic APIs have the same goal [3][16].
  • Latency. Anthropic still lists latency as limitation number one. It recommends computer use where speed is not critical, such as background research and automated testing [3].

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Pick the cheapest faithful observation. Use DOM or a11y references for web pages with reliable structure. Keep screenshots and zoom for verification and for surfaces structure cannot see. Pure pixels are for whole-desktop generality, not a default for web automation.
  2. Own the coordinate pipeline. Resize screenshots yourself to the model's pixel budget, keep a scale factor, and rescale every returned coordinate. Choose resolution so the smallest target you care about stays several pixels wide [3][5].
  3. Batch actions, but put barriers in. Allow multiple actions per turn. Stop at the first failure. Treat navigation as a barrier that ends the batch [3][25].
  4. Engineer the serializer, not just the prompt. Paint-order occlusion, containment deduplication, new-element markers, compact compound controls and password stripping are where DOM agents win or lose [24].
  5. Make completion a verified claim. Require evidence-backed subgoals or explicit verification before done. Use separate validator calls for high-value workflows [25][28].
  6. Compile what you have learned. Explore with an agent, then freeze working paths into deterministic code, cached act calls or selectors. Call the model again only when the site changes or a step fails [26][28].
  7. Spend test-time compute on trajectories. Best-of-N rollouts with a judge raised OSWorld scores by about 6 points for Agent S3. This needs environments you can snapshot and fork [34].
  8. Manage context like a cache. Keep a few recent screenshots, prune in batches aligned with cache breakpoints, compact at a threshold, and keep long-horizon state in files rather than in images [5][25].
  9. Assume prompt injection will happen. Use a fresh low-privilege profile, network-level domain allowlists that are re-checked after redirects, disabled javascript_exec and file upload by default, classifiers on untrusted content, and human confirmation for irreversible actions. Never pass secrets to the model; use takeover, observe-style selectors, or credential vaults [4][7][8][14][26][27].
  10. Distrust single benchmark numbers. Check the benchmark version (OSWorld vs. Verified vs. 2.x), the step limit, the scoring rule (binary vs. partial), the judge, and who ran the evaluation. The same model can differ by 9 or more points between harnesses [10][18][31][41].
  11. Mix modalities per step. The strongest products route each step to the cheapest capable channel: an API or connector, a shell, a text browser, an a11y-tree browser, or pixel control. ChatGPT agent's design and Claude's computer-plus-bash setup both reflect this [6][15].
